items.body:
## Scope correction (2026-10-29, after review)

The double read described here is **introduced by `#642`**, which is still open (`abc6f8c5`, `merged_at: null`). On current `main` @ `69f40c9f` the cache-hit path still uses `sameIdentity` + `objectIdentity` and reads no bytes, so this is **not reproducible on `main` yet**. Tracked here so it is handled as soon as `#642` merges; the PR for this issue must branch from the post-`#642` `main`, not from `69f40c9f`.

## Reproduction (after `#642` merges)

Warm page cache, node v22.23.2, ext4; measure one `putWorkspaceFile` call that is a **cache hit** (file and stored object both unchanged, so the call returns the cached `DataRef`):

| file size | metadata-only path (pre-`#642`) | post-`#642` path (source hash + `verifyRef`) |
|---|---|---|
| 64 KiB | 0.067 / 0.159 ms | 1.202 / 2.225 ms |
| 1 MiB | 0.083 / 0.100 ms | 9.404 / 11.050 ms |
| 8 MiB | 0.094 / 0.111 ms | 68.317 / 71.872 ms |

(median / max, 25 iterations after 3 warm-ups; measured on `#642` tip `abc6f8c5`)

## Current behaviour vs expected (post-`#642`)

`putWorkspaceFile` reads and hashes **the whole source file** (`unchangedWorkspaceBytes`, `packages/cas/src/versioning.ts:137-143`) and then reads and hashes **the whole stored object again** (`verifyRef`, `packages/cas/src/versioning.ts:216-227`). The two halves cost the same — at 1 MiB the source hash is 4.591 ms, the object hash 4.682 ms — i.e. SHA-256 throughput, not syscall overhead.

Callers hit this on every execution: `services/runner/src/execution-manager.ts:96` snapshots the workspace after each shell execution, so **1 MiB of workspace artifacts costs ≈ +9.3 ms per execution** (300 MiB ≈ +2.6 s, linear from the rows above).

The source read must stay — `mtimeNs`/`ctimeNs` cannot detect a same-size in-place rewrite inside one timestamp tick (that is `#641`: 171/200 stale before the fix, 0/200 after). The **second** read is the avoidable half: the source digest already equals `ref.digest` at that point.

Expected: verify each object at most once per store instance, so a cache hit does not re-read the object on every call.

## Code evidence

- `packages/cas/src/versioning.ts:137-143` — `unchangedWorkspaceBytes()` streams the source through sha256, then calls `verifyRef(ref)`.
- `packages/cas/src/versioning.ts:216-227` — `verifyRef()` streams the stored object through sha256 again.
- `services/runner/src/execution-manager.ts:96` — per-execution `snapshotWorkspace` call site.

## Suggested red test (after `#642` merges)

```ts
test("a cache hit does not re-read the stored object on every call", async () => {
  // count reads on the store's object read path
  // put the same unchanged file twice through putWorkspaceFile
  // first call: only the source read; second call: object read count stays at 1
  assert.equal(objectReads, 1)
})
```

Run: `cd packages/cas && node --import tsx --test --test-name-pattern "cache hit does not re-read" src/versioning.test.ts`
On the post-`#642` tree the counter is 2, so this fails; it passes once verification is cached per object.

## Duplicate check (open + closed)

- `verifyRef` → `#642` (adds the read), `#250` (closed: reuse verified objects during *ref commits* — different path).
- `"snapshotWorkspace" performance` → 0 hits.
- `CAS verify cost` → `#230`/`#540` (closed, trajectory-commit cost), `#297` (closed, unrelated).
- No other open PR touches the `putWorkspaceFile` reuse path.

Measured and reported by ScienceDiscovery (Dev-2) on `#642` (`discussion_r4408197899`).
items.title: [Perf] Workspace cache hits verify the same file twice (≈9.3 ms per MiB per shell execution)

items.author: HugoXK
items.body:
## Reproduction

On a clean checkout of `main` @ `69f40c9f` where workspace packages have not been built:

```bash
cd apps/web
node_modules/.bin/tsx --test tests/*.test.ts tests/*.test.tsx
```

Result on this machine: **448 tests, 385 pass, 63 fail**, and every failure is the same module resolution error from the `.tsx` files:

```
Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module
'.../apps/web/node_modules/@sciencediscovery/operational-logging/dist/diagnostics.js'
imported from .../apps/web/src/ErrorDiagnosticActions.tsx
```

Single-test repro: `node_modules/.bin/tsx --test tests/AuthTokenPrompt.test.tsx` → exit 1, same error.

It goes away only after `packages/operational-logging` is built (`tsc -p packages/operational-logging/tsconfig.json`), i.e. the web suite silently depends on a build step that its own `test` script does not perform.

## Current behaviour vs expected

`packages/operational-logging/package.json` maps the runtime entry to a build artifact:

```json
"exports": {
  ".":             { "types": "./src/index.ts",       "default": "./dist/index.js" },
  "./diagnostics": { "types": "./src/diagnostics.ts", "default": "./dist/diagnostics.js" }
}
```

Types resolve to `src/`, but the runtime entry resolves to `dist/`, so an unbuilt tree makes `apps/web` (which depends on this package as `workspace:*`, `apps/web/package.json:13`) fail at import time. `apps/web`'s `test` script is plain `tsx --test tests/*.test.ts tests/*.test.tsx` and has no build step; CI passes only because the pipeline builds first.

Expected: `apps/web` tests run on a clean checkout without a manual build of the workspace dependency — either the in-repo runtime entry points at the TS source (tsx/vite compile it) or the test script builds what it needs.

## Code evidence

- `packages/operational-logging/package.json` — `exports["./diagnostics"].default` = `./dist/diagnostics.js` while `types` = `./src/diagnostics.ts`; no `dist/` in the repository.
- `apps/web/package.json:13` — `"@sciencediscovery/operational-logging": "workspace:*"`.
- `apps/web/package.json` scripts — `"test": "tsx --test tests/*.test.ts tests/*.test.tsx"` (no build).
- Failure site: `apps/web/src/ErrorDiagnosticActions.tsx` imports `@sciencediscovery/operational-logging/diagnostics`.

## Suggested red test / acceptance

No new unit test is needed — the red state is the suite itself:

```bash
rm -rf packages/operational-logging/dist
cd apps/web && node_modules/.bin/tsx --test tests/*.test.ts     # ts files pass today
cd apps/web && node_modules/.bin/tsx --test tests/*.test.tsx    # 63 ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND today
```

Acceptance: with `dist/` absent, `tsx --test tests/*.test.tsx` reports **0 `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`** and the same pass count as with a built tree (448/448 on the tree where this was measured).

## Duplicate check (open + closed)

- `"operational-logging"` → no issue about its `exports` map or the missing build step.
- `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` → 0 hits in issues.
- `apps/web test` / web suite build → no open issue; `#467` is a UI fix, `#632` a feature.
- No open PR changes `packages/operational-logging/package.json` or the `apps/web` test script.

Found and measured by ScienceDiscovery while prewarming the web worktree for the `#646` sprint (448 tests, 63 `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` failures, worktree unmodified).
items.title: [Bug] apps/web test suite dies on a clean tree: 63/448 tests hit ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for the unbuilt operational-logging dist

items.author: qingkwl
items.body:
## Summary

This issue is the **platform layer** of the Windows desktop delivery (#400): the OS-adaptation seams in three core packages that everything else builds on — process-tree termination and owner-only file semantics in the runner, atomic replace and at-rest secret protection in the api, and directory durability plus MAX_PATH-safe lock names in the cas. It also carries the Windows build guide and the one-line CI fix that makes source paths readable on Windows.

It is the platform half of the work the closed #478 carried inside an oversized PR, re-landed per that review's feedback. The runtime behavior that consumes these seams (startup chain, execution router, micromamba, fail-closed permissions) is tracked separately and stacks on this one.

## Where the packages stand today

| Package | Current state on Windows |
|---|---|
| `services/runner` | Killing a child with POSIX signals leaves the whole process tree alive (#482); `chmod 0600` only toggles the read-only bit on NTFS; conda helpers assume a Linux layout. |
| `services/api` | Atomic replace via rename fails transiently under AV/indexer locks (EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY); at-rest secret protection has no Windows story — `0600` means nothing on NTFS (#400: "model keys are stored with DPAPI" on Windows). |
| `packages/cas` | `fsync` on a directory handle is EPERM; a 64-hex lock digest overruns MAX_PATH once SQLite appends `-journal`, failing `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` with `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`. |
| Build | No Windows build guide; `check-architecture.mjs` prints backslash paths on Windows. |

## Goals

- Every package gets a `platform/` facade: `types.ts` (the surface), `index.ts` (single dispatch point), `posix.ts` (transparent passthrough), `win32.ts` (the Windows implementation), plus `node:test` suites — the structure #400 prescribes ("per-package platform adapters, win32 and darwin side by side, single entry point, module boundaries enforced").
- Consumer call sites route through the facade only; no platform branches outside `platform/`.
- POSIX behavior unchanged everywhere, by construction (passthrough).
- The api master key is DPAPI-wrapped on win32 and restricted to its owner.

## Non-goals

- Consumer-level behavior (router, environments, permissions) — separate issue stacking on this one.
- macOS/darwin adapters — same facade shape, but darwin work is its own issue.
- Windows CI jobs (same gap as #482; evidence below is real-machine).

## Root decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Facade shape | `platform/` per package with a single dispatch point | #400's "Expected new components" prescribes exactly this shape; module boundaries stay enforceable by `check-architecture`. |
| CAS lock names | posix keeps the historical 64-hex digest; win32 shortens to 128 bits | Compatibility: coordination files written by main keep working on Linux; on Windows there are no existing files, and MAX_PATH headroom is required (SQLite `-journal` suffix). |
| CAS directory durability | posix fsync; win32 documented no-op | NTFS has no directory-fsync semantics; durability relies on volume-level policy. #478's review asked for the docs to state this — both languages do. |
| API secret protection | DPAPI on win32, identity on posix, self-describing blob prefix | #400: "model keys are stored with DPAPI" on Windows; no persisted blobs exist in main, so no compatibility promise is needed. |
| Runner termination | `taskkill /T /F` on win32, SIGKILL passthrough on posix | #482's design; verified end-to-end on a live child+grandchild pair. |

## Delivery

- `services/runner/src/platform/` — `terminateTree`, `restrictToOwner` (icacls), conda delay-load DLL paths and m2-bash shell location; `killSandboxProcess` and server-side 0600 semantics route through the facade.
- `services/api/src/platform/os/` — `restrictToOwner` (SID-based icacls grantee), `renameReplace` (retry/backoff), `wrapSecret`/`unwrapSecret`/`isWrappedSecret` (DPAPI); `loadOrCreateModelSecretKey` persists through the facade and restricts the key file.
- `packages/cas/src/platform/` — directory durability, `lockFileName`; versioning/workspace-lease/workspace-lifecycle route through the facade; docs (EN+ZH) note the Windows semantics.
- `scripts/build-windows.md` + `check-architecture.mjs` forward-slash fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All eight platform/secrets suites pass on a real Windows host, including a DPAPI round-trip and a tree-kill against a live child+grandchild pair.
- [ ] The cas lock name keeps the historical digest on posix (existing coordination files stay valid).
- [ ] No platform branches outside `platform/` beyond the minimal call-site hooks.
- [ ] POSIX behavior identical to main (passthrough by construction).
- [ ] `pnpm -r typecheck` green.

## Open questions

1. Should a `check-architecture` rule codify "tree-kill/signal call sites must not bypass `platform/`" (the AC3 refinement #482's triage suggested), making this enforceable in CI rather than by review?
2. Windows CI remains absent (#482 finding 4) — is a `windows-latest` job acceptable before more Windows-facing code lands?

## Related

- Parent: #400
- Runner facade implements the runner half of #482; api/cas facades re-land #477/#491 per the closed #478/#492 review feedback
- The runtime consumers (startup chain, execution router, micromamba, permissions) stack on this issue
items.title: [Feature] Windows platform adaptation facades (runner / api / cas) + build support + DPAPI secrets

items.author: qingkwl
items.body:
## Summary

This issue is the **runtime layer** of the Windows desktop delivery (#400): everything that makes the stack actually *run* on Windows once the platform facades exist — a native startup chain, an execution-provider routing layer, win-64 scientific environments, and fail-closed permission semantics for unsandboxed execution.

It implements the "Windows: an execution-provider routing layer" section of #400's execution model, and it is the runtime half of the work that the closed #478 carried inside an oversized PR. The platform seams it builds on (runner/api/cas facades, DPAPI secrets, build support) land separately as #639; this issue starts where that one ends.

## Where the stack stands today

| Area | Current state |
|---|---|
| Startup | `start-stack` orchestration and the JiuwenSwarm launcher are bash-centric; probing is slow and serial; uv trampolines break venv entry resolution on Windows; there is no packaged-stack mode for an NSIS payload. |
| Execution capability | Hardcoded to sandboxed providers (`bubblewrap`/`seatbelt`); the capability probe answers "unavailable" on Windows and nothing can execute. |
| Scientific environments | Environment provisioning assumes a Linux conda layout; no win-64 micromamba management, no starter environments. |
| Unsandboxed fallback | Nothing: without a sandbox there is no workspace confinement, no network policy, and no approval tightening — a silent security downgrade, which #400's baseline forbids. |

## Goals

- `scripts/start-stack.mjs` runs the whole stack natively on Windows (no WSL dependency), in both source and packaged mode.
- `packages/execution-router` answers "where does code run" on Windows, per #400: capability probing that assumes nothing, hot refresh, and a downgrade hook that tightens approval modes.
- Managed micromamba win-64 starter environments so direct execution can run Python out of the box.
- Unsandboxed execution is fail-closed: workspace allowlist, deny-all default network with audited refusals, persistent-shell guard, server-side approval tightening.
- POSIX behavior unchanged: sandboxed providers remain the Linux default and no posix path changes.

## Non-goals

- Provider B (the WSL sandbox plugin) itself — its rootfs, import state machine, and plugin center are a separate issue; here it stays a stub the router can register later.
- The remote provider (C) and macOS work.
- Any change to the existing `bubblewrap`/`seatbelt` enum semantics on Linux.
- Windows CI coverage (same gap as #482 — the evidence below is real-machine).

## Root decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Routing layer placement | Layered **on top of** the sandbox enum, never inside it | #400's root decision: "new code is layered on top, so upstream merges continue to apply". The enum stays three-valued for sandboxed providers; `"none"` is the Windows direct-execution entry. |
| Startup orchestration | Windows-native `.mjs` chain (`stack-platform.mjs` platform dispatch + `jiuwenswarm.mjs` launcher) | Windows "covered without WSL being mandatory" (#400); a bash-free chain also survives GBK consoles and paths with spaces. |
| Scientific environments | micromamba win-64, starter environments pinned in the repo | The bundled starter environment is what makes M1's "never touching WSL" exit criterion reachable; on-demand-only would fail the ≤1 min first-run budget. |
| Unsandboxed semantics | Fail-closed everywhere, approval locked to ask-on-dangerous on downgrade | #400's security baseline: "treats anything indeterminate as unavailable rather than routing on unknown state"; the downgrade hook reuses setApprovalMode's Permission Epoch semantics so the lock is server-side. |
| Ephemeral vs persistent shell | Ephemeral shell through the environment's m2-bash; persistent sessions refuse without a sandbox | `run_shell` is bash-syntax and the model depends on it (#400: "the bundled starter environment includes a bash compatibility layer"); persistent workers are the sandbox's job, so they wait for Provider B. |

## Delivery

### Startup chain

`scripts/lib/stack-platform.mjs` (single platform dispatch), `scripts/jiuwenswarm.mjs` (wall-clock deadline, TCP-first probing, exec timeouts, heartbeat logging, first-start diagnostics, uv-trampoline bypass via `entry_points.txt`, lazy start, `SCIENCE_AGENT_ENVS_DIR`), `scripts/start-stack.mjs` (native orchestration incl. packaged-stack mode for the NSIS payload). Both launcher and platform layer carry `node:test` suites.

### Execution router

`packages/execution-router`: provider registry, capability probing that reuses the runner's `/execution-capability` and `/health` (no new wire format), and the provider-downgrade hook — when the sandbox is lost, every `always_allow` session is tightened to `ask_for_dangerous` through `setApprovalMode` + `publishApprovalModeChange`. Wired into api bootstrap and `POST /api/execution-provider`.

### Micromamba environments

Environment-store platform hooks (win-64 starter specs, interpreter paths, package-install guidance with win-64 alternatives), launcher preflight, `SandboxKind "none"` in the schema, and `scripts/fetch-managed-micromamba.mjs` win-64 pinning.

### Fail-closed permissions

Workspace whitelist via `SCIENCE_RUNNER_EXTRA_WORKSPACE_ROOTS`; the default network policy is a deny-all gateway with audited denials; persistent shell refuses without a sandbox; ephemeral shell runs through the environment's m2-bash; readiness reports `"none"` honestly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a Windows host without WSL: `start-stack` brings port 4310 healthy natively, and the runner executes a Python task in the micromamba starter environment.
- [ ] The router probes capability at startup, caches it, refreshes on demand, and never routes on indeterminate state.
- [ ] Losing the sandbox tightens every `always_allow` session to `ask_for_dangerous`, server-side.
- [ ] Unsandboxed execution is confined to the workspace allowlist; default-policy network is deny-all with logged refusals.
- [ ] Persistent shell sessions fail closed outside a sandbox; ephemeral shell works through m2-bash.
- [ ] POSIX behavior unchanged: Linux defaults and all sandboxed paths identical to main.
- [ ] Launcher and platform-layer test suites run green on Windows.

## Open questions

1. Windows CI remains absent (same as #482's finding 4) — the real-machine evidence in the PR covers it for now; should a `windows-latest` job be added before Provider B lands?
2. `pnpm-lock.yaml` gains the `@sciencediscovery/execution-router` workspace dependency; builds must run before tests import `dist/`. Is the CI build step's ordering guaranteed on all jobs?
3. When Provider B (WSL plugin) lands, should its registration reuse this router's stub slot verbatim, or should the plugin center own registration?

## Related

- Parent: #400 (delivery design — implements its execution model, startup, and security baseline for Windows)
- Foundation: #639 (platform facades; this issue is stacked on it)
- Supersedes the runtime half of the closed #478
- Runner tree-kill behavior follows #482
items.title: [Feature] Windows runtime: native startup chain, execution routing, micromamba environments, and fail-closed permissions

items.author: ink999107
items.body:
## Summary

This issue is the delivery design for shipping ScienceDiscovery as a **desktop application on Windows and macOS**: one installer, one window, a first-run wizard, and automatic updates — with the code-execution and sandbox story settled per platform.

It is the design-level follow-up to #34 (desktop window) and #31 (Windows support), and it answers the questions those two left open: which shell framework, what to do about a Windows sandbox, how macOS gets a binary plus signing and notarization, and how updates reach installed apps. It also supplies the update mechanism asked for in #32.

## Where the product stands today

| Platform | Current state |
|---|---|
| Linux | Released binary and source mode; the UI is a browser tab on `127.0.0.1:4310`, reached with a bearer token. |
| macOS | Source mode only, officially supported on macOS 13+; sandbox is native (Seatbelt). No binary, no installer, no signing or notarization. |
| Windows | Not supported in any form. The existing `bubblewrap` + seccomp sandbox is Linux-only, and the runner, startup script, and binary packaging all assume a Linux or Darwin host. |

The practical effect: getting to a first screen means a terminal, a token copy-paste, and a browser tab, and a large group of researchers is excluded outright.

## Goals

- Download → install → wizard → working workspace, with no terminal, no token handling, and no manual environment setup.
- Windows covered without WSL being mandatory.
- Code execution stays inside the security contract the project already states, on both platforms.
- One shell codebase, one packaging pipeline, one release pipeline for both platforms.
- Installed apps keep themselves current.

## Non-goals for v1

- No Linux desktop build (Linux stays binary + browser).
- No forked frontend: the shell loads the same `apps/web` build against the same control API.
- No remote-execution provider on macOS. The remote link itself is cross-platform; only the Linux-hosted target ships with v1.
- No multi-instance support. Ports stay fixed and unique.
- No enterprise deployment formats (no Windows MSI, no macOS pkg).

## Root decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Shell | Electron, shared by both platforms | Same runtime family as the Node backend, identical rendering engine on every platform (the UI leans on Molstar, Plotly, Cytoscape), and the window, token injection, wizard, and orderly shutdown come for free. ~200 MB of memory is the accepted cost. |
| Execution environment | Windows: provider-based, direct execution by default, WSL and remote demoted to optional plugins. macOS: Seatbelt by default, fail-closed if unavailable, no remote. | On Windows the sandbox was always an interchangeable provider, so WSL becomes a plugin rather than the foundation — users who cannot install WSL are not shut out. On macOS the sandbox is already built into the OS and available on probe. |
| Bundling | Layered | Base package ~500–700 MB and works offline; large pieces (the WSL rootfs on Windows, heavy scientific dependencies) ship as on-demand plugin volumes; macOS ships per-architecture packages. |
| Architecture matrix | Windows: x64 only, tiered by OS version. macOS: 13+, arm64 as the mainline plus an x64 build. | Windows arm64 volumes do not justify the work yet, and direct execution has no hard WSL dependency, so older Windows versions remain covered. On macOS the conda scientific stack splits by architecture and a CPython/conda environment cannot be a universal binary. |
| Ordering | Windows is the first target platform, macOS the second. | Sharing the shell, packaging, and release pipeline costs the least when done once; macOS needs no backend adaptation and has a native sandbox, so it can reach internal beta sooner. |

## Execution model

### Shared

SD already models isolation as a replaceable enum — `bubblewrap` on Linux, `seatbelt` on macOS, chosen automatically by the backend. The desktop work adds a second, orthogonal question: **where** code runs.

### Windows: an execution-provider routing layer

- A routing layer above the existing sandbox enum answers "where does code run" with `windows-direct | wsl | remote`. The two layers stay independent: routing to WSL still isolates with bubblewrap inside it; routing to direct execution falls back to the approval mode because Windows has no OS-level sandbox. The existing enum does not change — new code is layered on top, so upstream merges continue to apply.
- **Capability probing, fail-closed.** The router assumes nothing about the machine: at startup it checks whether WSL is present, whether the private sandbox instance has been imported, and whether a remote host is configured. This reuses the existing sandbox-probe mechanism, caches the result for the session, and treats anything indeterminate as unavailable rather than routing on unknown state.
- **Hot switching.** Finishing a plugin install re-probes without restarting the backend. A persistent badge shows the active mode: sandboxed, direct, or remote.
- **Direct execution path.** The `run_shell` tool is bash-syntax and the model depends on it, so the bundled starter environment includes a bash compatibility layer (the MSYS2 port). Without it, direct execution could not run code at all.
- **Provider B (WSL plugin).** A trimmed, purpose-built Linux rootfs (~200 MB: bash, bubblewrap, system libraries, python3) imported under a dedicated instance name via `wsl --import`, bypassing the Store and its 1–2 GB download. Installation is a six-step state machine (detect → platform install → rootfs import → dependency check → network check → payload placement) with a journal after each step so an interrupted install resumes. A redistribution-compliance review of the Ubuntu base is required before this work starts; if it does not clear, the base moves to Debian.
- **No dead ends.** If the plugin cannot be installed, the user keeps direct execution, gets a specific failure reason with illustrated guidance, and has one-click rollback. Uninstalling the plugin deregisters the instance, clears the rootfs, and returns to direct execution with no residue.

### macOS: native sandbox, no routing layer

- macOS is a Unix platform; the backend stack already runs there in source mode, and Seatbelt is built in. The three heaviest pieces of the Windows plan — backend adaptation, the provider routing layer plus WSL plugin system, and the unsandboxed fallback — disappear or shrink sharply here.
- The default tier **is** the full sandbox. There are no plugins to install and no mode to switch; the mode badge stays visible and reads "sandboxed".
- If Seatbelt is unavailable (MDM-managed machines, nested sandboxing), the app fails closed with an explicit error and diagnostics. It does not degrade to unsandboxed execution the way Windows does.

## Packaging, signing, and distribution

| Area | Windows | macOS |
|---|---|---|
| Toolchain | electron-builder — one configuration produces both platform targets | same |
| Installer | NSIS, per-user install under `%LocalAppData%\Programs`, no UAC elevation anywhere | Standard DMG drag to `/Applications`; no permission special-casing |
| Artifact naming | `ScienceDiscovery-<version>-win-x64-setup.exe` | `ScienceDiscovery-<version>-mac-<arch>.dmg`, plus `.zip` as the update carrier and a per-arch `latest-mac.yml` |
| Signing | Current version is unsigned. The next version may add Azure Trusted Signing (OIDC short-lived credentials in CI, no certificate on disk). Identity validation is officially ~3–5 business days and can stretch to weeks if materials are bounced, so the application has to start early. | Public distribution requires Developer ID + notarization (notarytool) + stapling. Internal beta may ship ad-hoc with `xattr -cr` guidance, switching to the notarized chain as soon as it is ready. Apple account and certificate lead time applies. |
| Runtime pinning | — | The macOS build needs a pinned runtime manifest: CPython (both architectures), uv (mac wheel), micromamba (osx-arm64/osx-64), and the starter environment, all by version and hash. Today the manifest pins Linux only. |
| Distribution | All downloads are GitHub Releases assets. The website `/install` page is the primary entry point and the Releases page the secondary one; both link the same assets. No domestic object storage or custom domain. Plugin packages ship the same way. | `/install` shows two download cards and pre-selects the architecture by user agent, with manual override. |
| Updates | electron-updater reading Releases assets, stable channel only to start, `latest.yml` + blockmap for delta updates. | The zip is the update carrier: electron-updater downloads the notarized zip, replaces the `.app`, and restarts. The DMG is not part of the update flow. |
| Update-source stability | The update URL is fixed from the first public release, because installed apps have it baked in. | same |
| Interception | SmartScreen: unsigned cold starts are accepted for now, with documented "More info → Run anyway" guidance. | Gatekeeper: notarization plus stapling removes the prompt entirely; no user guidance is needed once that chain is live. |

## First run

- Three-step wizard: data directory → model configuration (preset provider → API key → live connectivity test) → done.
- On Windows the wizard goes through direct execution only: no environment preparation, no WSL involvement.
- On macOS the final step folds in the sandbox self-check. A failure shows a specific error page with diagnostics and a way to submit them, and **does not** let the user into the main UI. Ordinary users never see this page.
- Data directory defaults: Windows splits by provider — direct execution uses `%LocalAppData%`, WSL uses ext4 inside the instance for I/O performance — with a custom option and a free-space check. macOS uses `~/Library/Application Support/ScienceDiscovery` and offers a one-time migration when a source-mode `~/.sciencediscovery-data` is found.
- Model keys: Windows stores them with DPAPI, because `0600` file permissions mean nothing on NTFS. macOS keeps the existing AES-256-GCM + `0600` scheme.
- The access token is injected before the page loads; a token entry page appears only as a 401 fallback.
- Background work during first run (environment unpacking, stack start) reports real progress by file and byte count, with conservative time estimates, and gates the next step on a self-check.

## Security baseline

Shared:

- Workspace-directory allowlist; network calls require explicit authorization (egress denied by default, allowlist to permit, refusals recorded).
- A persistent badge in the UI states the execution mode.
- Supply chain: updates over HTTPS with integrity checks (sha512 in the Windows update manifest; same-chain signing and notarization for the macOS update zip). **Once signing is live, no unsigned version is published again**, and a signature-identity change is covered by a dual-identity transition window.

Windows direct execution (no sandbox):

- The permission mode is locked to "ask on dangerous operations" and the user cannot switch to "always allow". This is enforced server-side, so a modified frontend cannot bypass it. Usability is unaffected: safe operations never prompt, and dangerous-operation prompts offer "allow once" or "allow matching", so approving a class of operation stops repeated prompts.
- The stack is not multi-instance: fixed ports, loopback-only listeners; a port occupied by an unknown process is reported honestly rather than worked around.

## Compatibility

Windows:

| OS | Direct execution | WSL plugin |
|---|---|---|
| Windows 11 22H2+ | yes | yes (inbox component; mirrored networking available) |
| Windows 10 2004+ | yes | yes (`wsl --install --no-distribution`) |
| Windows 10 1909 and older | yes, degraded | no — explicit "not installable" message |

macOS: 13+ on arm64 (mainline — CI smoke and e2e run here) and 13+ on x64 (package plus lightweight validation); macOS 12 and older unsupported, matching the existing source-mode floor.

Known environmental constraints to handle explicitly:

- Windows path length (260 characters) versus deep Python package trees: guide toward a shallow data directory, keep the environment root shallow, truncate over-long filenames.
- Windows antivirus tools interrupting file writes during install and update, producing incomplete installs; unsigned builds add SmartScreen on top. Document allowlisting and maintain a known-issues library.
- Windows defaulting to GBK on Chinese systems: every script must specify UTF-8 explicitly.
- macOS App Translocation and the quarantine flag before notarization: both are resolved by signing, notarizing, and stapling.
- Missing Apple Silicon builds for a minority of packages: guide users to pip.

## Non-functional budgets

| Metric | Budget | Target |
|---|---|---|
| First run, fresh install to usable main UI | ≤1 min, both platforms | Windows ~30 s on SSD (environment ships in the package, so the cost is unpacking plus stack start); macOS near-instant |
| Packaged stack start | fast | port 4310 healthy within 30 s, both platforms |
| Minor-version update | delta only | Windows blockmap delta; macOS zip delta |
| WSL plugin install | real progress, conservative estimate | rootfs import plus dependency check within a fixed bound once the first release has data |

Memory: on Windows with the WSL plugin active, write `.wslconfig` limits (4 GB / 4 processors, adjustable in the wizard) so `vmmem` cannot take half the host. Direct execution has no `vmmem`. macOS needs no mechanism. The ~200 MB Electron shell is accepted on both.

## Process model

Three kinds of process, managed by one Electron main process:

| Process | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Electron main | Native window and OS integration (Windows: tray and system menu; macOS: application menu, Cmd+Q / Cmd+W); backend lifecycle (probe, start, clean shutdown); injects the access token before page load. |
| Renderer | The existing web UI; on first run it renders the bundled local wizard page first, then the main UI. |
| Backend stack | adapter (Python front door) + API (Node, business logic) + runner (code execution: the routing target on Windows, the sandbox execution point on macOS); memory-graph, evolve, and JiuwenSwarm start on demand. |

Startup: renderer wizard first (it needs no backend) → health probe every 3 s, reusing an already-healthy stack left over from a crash instead of starting a second one → otherwise start the stack → load the UI once the stack is healthy. Request path: page → adapter `:4310` → API `:4410` → runner `:4311`. Shutdown waits for running tasks, then stops only the children this process started; a reused stack is left alone. On Windows the window minimizes to the tray by default and closing it asks for confirmation when tasks are running; on macOS closing the window keeps the application and the backend alive, matching the backend semantics that a run continues after the page is closed.

Updates: checked at startup and every 6 hours; notify, download only on confirmation, never silently upgrade in the background. Installation first waits for running tasks and confirms all child processes have exited.

## Expected new components

- `client/shell/` — the Electron shell (shared; main process branches on platform, preload handles token injection and wizard IPC, `wizard.html` and `fallback.html` are platform-neutral).
- `packages/execution-router/` — the Windows execution-provider routing layer (no macOS counterpart).
- `packages/*/platform/` — per-package platform adapters (win32 and darwin side by side, single entry point, module boundaries enforced), e.g. a secret protector that uses DPAPI on Windows and AES-256-GCM + `0600` on macOS.
- `packages/sandbox-capability/` — extend the existing probe and runtime manifest with macOS entries.
- `scripts/start-stack.mjs` — packaged stack entry point, plus `stack-platform.mjs` for platform differences.
- `build/assemble-backend.mjs`, `build/resources/`, `build/rootfs/` — backend assembly (Windows x64 and per-arch macOS), the extraResources volume, and the trimmed WSL rootfs build (Windows only).
- `scripts/binary-release/runtimes.json` — add the darwin section.
- `.github/workflows/` — add Windows and `macos-14` (arm64) jobs for packaging (macOS including signing and notarization) and platform regression.

## Delivery milestones

| Milestone | Platform | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | Windows | Download page → setup.exe → wizard → complete a small task with SD, never touching WSL. |
| M2 | Windows | On a machine without WSL: one-click sandbox install from the plugin center → run a sandboxed task → uninstall and fall back. |
| M3 | macOS | Source stack plus shell loading 4310 (backend ready, sandbox native — if the shell runs, this works). |
| M4 | macOS | Signed and notarized DMG, double-click to use: fresh Mac → download → drag install → wizard → complete a small task with no Gatekeeper prompt at any point. |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Windows: a fresh machine installs and completes a task without WSL installed.
- [ ] Windows: the sandbox plugin installs in one click, resumes after interruption, and can be uninstalled cleanly.
- [ ] Windows: direct execution cannot be switched to "always allow", and the lock holds when the client is modified.
- [ ] macOS: a signed, notarized DMG opens with no Gatekeeper prompt and no `xattr` workaround.
- [ ] macOS: when Seatbelt is unavailable, startup fails closed with diagnostics instead of running unsandboxed.
- [ ] Both: first run reaches a usable UI within the stated budget on a fresh install.
- [ ] Both: an update lands as a delta, never silently, and never while a task is running.
- [ ] Both: the shell loads the existing `apps/web` build — no forked frontend.
- [ ] Both: quitting leaves no orphaned stack processes, and a reused stack is not stopped.

## Open questions

1. Is an Apple Developer identity available to the project for Developer ID signing and notarization? Public macOS distribution cannot ship without it, and the account lead time is real.
2. Do we start the Azure Trusted Signing application now so the next Windows version can be signed? If the answer is yes, the application has to begin ahead of the release.
3. When do we add a distribution path that is reliable from mainland China? GitHub asset downloads are workable but not dependable, and the update source is fixed once the first public release ships.
4. The shell is expected to live outside the main repository's git history. Is that acceptable to the maintainers, or should it live in-tree?
5. Telemetry is scoped to a minimal, in-app-disableable set with a published collection list (install success rate, first-run completion, Windows provider distribution and plugin install step outcomes, macOS architecture distribution, Seatbelt probe failure rate). Does that list pass review?
items.title: [Feature] Ship the Windows and macOS desktop client - delivery design for packaging, execution, signing, and updates

items.body:
Follow-up to #617. This issue tracks **only** the CI packaging that #617 currently carries; it does not re-open the product fix in that PR.

## Trigger

Do not implement this until the maintainers answer the CI-contract question on #617 (comment `6463813036`):

- **A — accept as written**: the packaging stays in #617; close this issue with that reason and make no pipeline change.
- **B — split (our preference)**: #617 is reduced to the product fix, and one PR implements this issue.

If the answer is A, this issue is closed rather than implemented.

## Scope (only if B)

- `real-e2e.yml`: the always-run `Summarize model wire diagnostics` step and the `model-wire-summary.json` staging.
- `.ci/model-wire-summary.mjs` and its test; `prepare-real-e2e-results.mjs` staging; the `real-report.mjs` report section; `.ci/README.md`; the `ci-contract.test.mjs` expectation bump.

Out of scope: the empty-terminal-turn product fix and the wire-diagnostics fields (they stay in #617), and the relay-vs-direct measurement (criterion 3 of #245, tracked in #618).

## Merge condition

A test must exercise the real parse path: feed `[model-sse-summary]` lines as the emitters actually write them through the aggregation and staging path, and assert the resulting document. Hand-built records are not acceptance for that script.

## Context

The packaging is additive evidence — it reports model-wire failures next to research outcomes and does not add a second pass/fail gate. Splitting it keeps a default-branch pipeline change out of a behaviour fix and removes the "contract test edited to expect the change it guards" objection.

items.author: qingkwl
items.body:
## Problem

The desktop model picker (wizard step 3 and 设置 → 模型) is currently a native `<select>` over the provider's preset list plus a separate "custom" option: picking a model means scrolling the dropdown, and entering a custom model id means switching to the custom option first and then typing.

With longer preset lists (multi-page provider catalogs), the select has no way to search or filter, and the two-step custom flow makes quick overrides heavier than they need to be.

## Expected

A combobox-style model picker:

1. Typing filters the preset list live (match on id and display name).
2. Full keyboard navigation: ArrowUp/ArrowDown to move, Enter to commit, Esc to close without changing.
3. Free-text values stay first-class: a typed id that matches no preset is offered as a custom value directly (no mode switch).
4. Opening the dropdown shows the full unfiltered list (the current value does not pre-filter it).

We have a working implementation of this component (`ModelComboBox`, a self-contained React component + its styles) running on our Windows desktop branch; it was originally built to replace a `datalist`-based picker that had two platform bugs (the list filtered itself to the current value, and the indicator sat low), but it applies equally well as an upgrade over the `<select>`.

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — search narrows, value does not

Preconditions: provider with a preset list > 10 models, one already selected.
Steps: Open the picker; observe the list; type a substring.
Expected / pass: The dropdown initially shows all presets; typing narrows the list; reopening always starts unfiltered.

### Case 2 — keyboard-only round trip

Steps: Focus the field; ArrowDown/ArrowUp; Enter; Esc while open.
Expected / pass: Selection commits on Enter, cancels cleanly on Esc (no dialog close, no value change).

### Case 3 — custom value without mode switch

Steps: Type an id that matches no preset; commit.
Expected / pass: The value is accepted as a custom model id (same validation path as the current custom flow).

## Related

- Parent: #400 (Ship the Windows and macOS desktop client)
- Design discussion first; implementation follows as a PR if the direction is agreed.
items.title: [Feature] Searchable model picker (combobox) for the desktop wizard and settings

items.author: qingkwl
items.body:
## Problem

When the desktop stack runs against the JiuwenSwarm backend, `services/api` currently forces `store.useEverySkillEverywhere()` on startup whenever a JiuwenSwarm instance is configured (`services/api/src/http/index.ts`, the `jiuwenSwarm` branch). The effect: every installed skill is enabled for every project regardless of what the user selects.

The desktop UI still shows per-project skill selection (settings page + per-project toggles), but under this backend the selection is stored and never applied — a silent no-op from the user's perspective.

## Expected

Per-project skill selection should keep working under the JiuwenSwarm backend, or at minimum the forced-everywhere behavior should be an explicit, documented choice rather than an unconditional override.

Proposed design direction (open for discussion):

1. Replace the unconditional `useEverySkillEverywhere()` with a configuration switch, e.g. `SD_SKILL_SCOPE` (or an equivalent settings key) with values:
   - `everywhere` (current behavior; could remain the default during migration)
   - `project` (per-project selection drives what the agent run loads)
2. In `project` mode, the run payload resolves the project's `enabledSkillIds` and passes the resolved set to the JiuwenSwarm agent session, so the selection actually drives which skills the backend loads.
3. The UI keeps showing the truth: if scope is `everywhere`, per-project toggles should be disabled or annotated accordingly (the desktop already has the components for this).

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — project scope drives loading

Preconditions: JiuwenSwarm backend configured; scope = `project`; a project with a subset of skills selected.
Steps: Start an agent run in that project; inspect the skill set the JiuwenSwarm session loads.
Expected / pass: Only the selected skills are loaded; changing the project selection changes the loaded set on the next run.

### Case 2 — everywhere scope unchanged

Preconditions: scope = `everywhere` (default).
Steps: Same as Case 1.
Expected / pass: All installed skills load, matching today's behavior.

### Case 3 — no silent no-op

Preconditions: any scope.
Steps: Inspect the settings page rendering against the active scope.
Expected / pass: The UI never shows editable controls that have no effect.

## Related

- Parent: #400 (Ship the Windows and macOS desktop client)
- This is a design discussion first; the implementation PR follows the agreed switch semantics.
items.title: [Feature] Per-project skill selection under the JiuwenSwarm backend (scope switch design)

items.author: zy95-12
items.body:
## Problem

Successful real research runs still have a large per-case memory footprint for individual users. On current `feat/jiuwenswarm`, the highest observed worker cgroup peak is **11.12 GiB**. Although the latest GraphMemory fix prevented the previously observed runaway behavior in this experiment, this steady operational footprint deserves separate investigation and reduction for ordinary personal computers.

This is a resource-efficiency issue, not a report of another GraphMemory OOM. It is separate from #210 / its fix #212.

## Measured evidence

Experiment revision: `17d0774a` (includes #212 and TC Judge fix #209).

- Nine real scientific E2E cases, three repetitions each; four case workers concurrently.
- GraphMemory enabled throughout, local backend, isolated graph directory per case/repetition.
- Native task dispatch with Swarm execution; generator/Judge `deepseek-flash`.
- Each worker has a 24 GiB cgroup limit and no swap. The group includes the platform stack, graph service, Swarm, Runner and descendants, browser, and Judge.
- All 27 attempts delivered successfully. Retained `memory.events` show `max=0`, `oom=0`, `oom_kill=0` for every worker.

| Case / repetition | Worker cgroup peak (GiB) | Sampled Node API RSS peak (GiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TC-E2E-01 / 1 | 11.124 | 0.977 |
| DRB-75 / 1 | 11.123 | 1.127 |
| DRB-62 / 2 | 10.796 | 0.952 |
| DRB-75 / 3 | 10.397 | 1.275 |
| DRB-59 / 2 | 10.107 | 1.080 |

The three worker peaks for TC-E2E-01 were 11.12 / 8.27 / 8.43 GiB; DRB-75 was 11.12 / 8.61 / 10.40 GiB. Even PUCT's workers peaked around 4.41 GiB in this setup.

**Measurement boundaries:**

- Cgroup peak includes charged file cache and other memory, not just anonymous RSS. It is not proof that the application requires 11 GiB of unreclaimable working memory.
- API RSS is sampled separately and its maximum need not coincide with the group peak. Do not subtract these maxima to infer another component's usage.
- GraphMemory did not appear in the retained high-RSS process samples, but these contain only the host's top 12 processes above a threshold, so its precise individual peak cannot be recovered.
- This harness includes Playwright and diagnostic sampling. Startup/provisioning, browser, diagnostics, page cache, child agents, and runtime costs must be separated before attributing the footprint to the product or GraphMemory.
- Concurrent cases and agent choices varied; this is not a controlled concurrency-scaling measurement.

## Why this matters

Users on 8–16 GiB machines also need memory for the OS, browser, and other applications. Raising per-worker limits or recommending large-memory hosts is not an adequate resource-efficiency strategy. We need to establish the actual working set and provide a practical personal-machine configuration without silently dropping research evidence or quality requirements.

## Investigation and optimization plan

1. Record `memory.stat` (`anon`, `file`, `kernel`, `slab`, etc.), `memory.current/peak/events`, and memory pressure alongside process-tree attribution for the **specific worker cgroup**. Capture phase markers for startup, provisioning, child research, synthesis, and grading.
2. Sample process RSS/PSS by role: API, Swarm/gateway, graph, Runner/executions, browser, Judge. Keep diagnostics lightweight and credential-free; measure profiler overhead explicitly.
3. Reproduce TC-E2E-01 and DRB-75 alone and with concurrent child tasks. Measure the idle stack separately and compare with/without the browser/profiling overhead. Preserve GraphMemory and the same delivery/scoring contract.
4. Identify avoidable duplication or retention only from profiles: repeated runtime processes, scientific environments/imports, per-agent contexts, trajectory buffers, graph state, caches, and teardown. Do not assume any one is the culprit from aggregate peaks.
5. Optimize the dominant confirmed contributors. If required, provide explicit resource-aware concurrency/backpressure and document the latency tradeoff rather than changing research tasks or silently disabling capabilities.

## Acceptance criteria

- Produce a component/phase memory breakdown for the highest-footprint cases, distinguishing reclaimable cache from working memory.
- Establish a measured baseline and a concrete lower memory budget suitable for a representative personal machine, with headroom for OS and interactive use; do not invent a target before attribution.
- Demonstrate improvement against that baseline on the same tasks, with GraphMemory enabled, no OOM, retained artifact delivery, and quality scoring reported independently.
- Check memory release after task completion and repeated use within a long-lived session; include lightweight regression monitoring where practical.

Retained evidence on the experiment host (not publicly accessible):
`/root/sciencediscovery-real9-graph-3x-20260927/case-summary.csv`, plus each case's `memory.csv`, `memory-events.txt`, and `memory-profiles/memory-*.jsonl`.
items.title: [Feature] Reduce real research memory footprint for personal machines: worker peaks reach 11.12 GiB

items.author: zy95-12
items.body:
## Background and environment

During a source installation on a Debian 13 cloud desktop on 2026-10-11, using main commit `5ddaa38bd68a84e4e20b14116d91880fe87bdd08`, two problems required manual investigation:

1. The desktop terminal did not inherit the outbound proxy environment. The initial managed micromamba download failed with `ECONNREFUSED`; an installation environment with the required network configuration could complete the download.
2. When the adapter inherited a SOCKS proxy configuration, it failed to start because `socksio` was missing, affecting access to the application.

The first observation is an environment-triggered failure, not proof of a downloader implementation defect. The second has a concrete dependency declaration gap.

## Conditions and observed behavior

### A. Different proxy environments across installation and runtime entry points

- External access required a proxy, but the terminal initiating scientific-environment preparation did not inherit the corresponding configuration.
- The micromamba connection was refused and scientific-environment preparation could not complete.
- Installation succeeded through an official download/install path with the necessary network configuration, retaining the pinned version and SHA-256 verification.
- The scientific environment subsequently became ready, with Python 3.12, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and Matplotlib available.

### B. SOCKS configuration prevents adapter startup

- Create a clean adapter environment from the declared project dependencies and start it with a valid SOCKS proxy configuration.
- During HTTP client initialization, the missing socksio dependency prevents adapter startup.
- In this installation, adding socksio from official PyPI to the adapter's isolated environment restored startup; API health and page HTML checks then passed.

Source references:
- [Adapter declares plain httpx](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/5ddaa38bd68a84e4e20b14116d91880fe87bdd08/services/adapter/pyproject.toml#L19-L25).
- [HTTP clients are constructed during startup](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/5ddaa38bd68a84e4e20b14116d91880fe87bdd08/services/adapter/src/sciencediscovery_adapter/app.py#L47-L63).

## User impact

- Users may have already installed the source and other dependencies, yet still be blocked at first startup or scientific-environment preparation, preventing access to the workbench or relevant computations.
- Users must investigate differences between terminal and child-process proxy environments, and may need to install undeclared dependencies manually.
- A component-level failure can look like a failed installation of the entire application, leading to unnecessary reinstalls. This is not evidence that micromamba itself is unsuitable or unavailable.

## Expected behavior and proposed improvements

1. Unify installation/startup preflight checks: inspect the actual child process's proxy configuration, connectivity to required download sources, and dependencies for the selected proxy protocol. Report redacted status, never credentials.
2. Declare and lock SOCKS support, for example through `httpx[socks]`. Define the proxy boundary between loopback service calls and external requests, including correct `NO_PROXY` handling.
3. Identify the failing component, stage, underlying cause, and actionable next step. After configuration is corrected, allow retrying the failed step while reusing verified tools and caches.
4. Report Web entry point, adapter, and scientific-environment readiness separately instead of treating partial readiness as an all-or-nothing result.

The repository already has [download retry and cache mechanisms](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/5ddaa38bd68a84e4e20b14116d91880fe87bdd08/scripts/fetch-managed-micromamba.mjs#L179-L295), as well as [classified errors and mirror/preinstalled-tool recovery guidance](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/5ddaa38bd68a84e4e20b14116d91880fe87bdd08/services/runner/src/environment-store.ts#L1138-L1173). The goal is to connect these capabilities into a coherent first-run experience, not to replace the downloader.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A clean adapter environment starts with HTTP/SOCKS proxy configurations without manually installing undeclared dependencies.
- [ ] Missing or incorrect proxy configuration produces redacted, actionable diagnostics while retaining the underlying error.
- [ ] Correcting configuration allows retrying the failed step and reusing verified artifacts, without clearing all data or reinstalling.
- [ ] Version pinning and hash verification remain enforced; recovery does not disable TLS verification.
- [ ] Tests cover no proxy, HTTP/SOCKS proxies, unreachable download sources, and successful retry after correction; installation documentation is updated.

Related: #29 (actionable dependency preflight), #213 and #229 (onboarding feedback). This issue focuses on the observed proxy-related failures and first-install recovery experience.
items.title: [Bug] Improve proxy-aware installation: declare SOCKS support and unify preflight and recovery

items.author: zy95-12
items.body:
## 背景 / 输入

在本地 ScienceDiscovery（main 源码 serve，`http://127.0.0.1:4310`）用 NatureBench 论文复现 case：

- Case：`s43588-024-00689-2`（meK-means / multimodal clustering）
- 会话：`93f897ca-cefe-4e7b-932d-8339cbef1459`（项目「NatureBench meK-means 复现」）
- 宿主侧把任务数据以**绝对路径软链**放进 session workspace：
  - `naturebench_data` → `/workspace/NatureBench/data/naturebench_data/tasks/s43588-024-00689-2/problem/data`
  - `CGP_2023_ref` → `/workspace/CGP_2023`
- Agent 在沙箱内执行 `run.py` 读 loom / 作者代码

相关 run：`8164ed2d-8b42-4d67-9d4b-e47c12ce0f7e`（第一轮，约 23.6 min，仅 smoke）

## 问题是什么

会话沙箱里 `/workspace` 是 **session workspace 的 bind mount**，会遮蔽宿主上的 `/workspace/...`。因此指向宿主绝对路径的软链在沙箱内**解析失败**，真实 loom 不可达。

结果：Agent 只能合成 loom 做端到端 smoke，**真实 `output/{cl3,cl5,mop_*}/predictions.npy` 第一轮全部缺失**；报告写「blocked / NOT produced」。

## 我们怎么规避的

在**宿主**（沙箱外）把数据 materialize 成会话内相对目录，并删掉绝对软链：

```bash
cd …/sessions/<sid>/workspace
cp -a /workspace/NatureBench/.../problem/data nb_data
# 去掉指向宿主 /workspace 的断链软链
rm -f naturebench_data CGP_2023_ref
DATA_DIR=nb_data python run.py --data-dir nb_data
```

续跑后 cl3 / cl5 / mop_sc 真实 predictions 才落盘。

## 期望应该是什么样

1. 往 session workspace 放数据时，产品应 **materialize 或相对路径化**（或官方 `workspace_transfer`），**不要**依赖指向宿主绝对路径的软链。
2. UI / API 上传或「挂载外部目录」若最终进沙箱，应在创建时校验：沙箱内 `ls` 可读；失败则明确报错，而不是让 Agent 默默落到合成数据。
3. 文档写清：沙箱可见路径规则（相对 workspace、禁止宿主绝对软链）。

## 证据

- 第一轮报告结论与 `naturebench_data` → `/workspace/NatureBench/...` 软链
- 续跑 materialize `nb_data/` 后 cl3 `(902,)`、cl5 `(3918,)`、mop_sc `(5693,)` 真实 npy 成功

## 背景 / 输入

在 ScienceDiscovery 沙箱 / science-env 中复现 meK-means（Monod `mminference`）：

- 环境：`/opt/science-env/bin/python`
- 依赖：`monod==0.2.9.0`、`loompy`、`anndata`、较新的 `numpy`（≥2）

Case：`s43588-024-00689-2`；驱动脚本 `run.py`。

## 问题是什么

Monod 0.2.9.0 与 **numpy 2** 组合需要额外 shim 才能跑通作者路径，例如：

- `np.meshgrid` 返回值按 list 使用的兼容
- float bounds / `gridsize=[1,1]` 等调用约定修补

否则 Agent 卡在依赖/兼容调试，而不是论文复现本身。预装科学栈「开箱可跑作者代码」的承诺打折。

## 我们怎么规避的

在会话内自建/修补 `mekmeans-cpu` 路径与 shim（详见会话 `REPRODUCTION_REPORT.md` §3），再跑真实 loom。

## 期望应该是什么样

1. science-env（或官方 skill）对常见复现栈给出**钉死且测过的** monod/numpy/loompy 组合，或提供已知 shim 文档。
2. Agent 首次导入失败时，表面友好的「已知兼容问题 + 推荐 pin」提示，而不是长 traceback 试错。
3. 可选：NatureBench / 论文复现模板预装最小可跑镜像，与 brief 中的计算提示对齐。

items.author: HongyeZhou
items.body:
## Motivation

Long-running offline computations and Agent conversations have different lifecycles. An Agent turn can finish while a training, simulation, or batch-processing task continues running. After evaluation, this is a feature-design topic about coordination between offline tasks and Agents, rather than a defect in turn completion.

This issue replaces #434 and preserves its motivating scenario.

## Motivating scenario

In the NatureBench reproduction session `93f897ca-cefe-4e7b-932d-8339cbef1459`, run `84d71b8a-77dd-42a7-bc81-15e326b14cb1` completed while a background `python run.py --instances mop_sc` computation continued. The final computation took approximately 1,587.7 seconds and produced `predictions.npy` with shape `(5693,)`.

The user had to inspect host processes and wait for the output manually. Starting another Agent run could also launch duplicate work. An Agent promising to return after a wall-clock delay is not a reliable scheduling mechanism.

## Feature scope

Design how long-running offline tasks collaborate with Agents across turns:

- Give supported offline tasks a queryable identity and lifecycle, with ownership linked to the originating session/run.
- Make ongoing computation visible even after the initiating Agent turn finishes.
- Let a later turn inspect, await, or resume coordination with the same task without starting duplicate computation.
- Define how task completion, failure, cancellation, and results become available to the user and Agent.
- Define the default turn-completion policy when a task is still running, including whether explicit detachment is required.
- Document lifecycle limits, including runtime/service restarts and the treatment of processes launched outside the supported task mechanism.

## Design decisions before implementation

- Turn completion: wait for the task, require explicit detach, or register it in the background and notify.
- Ownership and persistence: session-level versus run-level handles, and restart behavior.
- Minimum user interface: how users discover active tasks, inspect progress, and retrieve results.
- Agent continuation: explicit user-driven await/resume versus automatic completion notification or continuation.
- Delivery decomposition: build on existing execution/query/wait capabilities and split implementation into reviewable changes.

These are open design questions; this issue does not select a policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- A user starts a representative long-running computation and can distinguish Agent-turn completion from task completion.
- The same supported task remains discoverable and queryable across turns according to the documented lifecycle.
- The Agent can inspect or await that task and retrieve its final result without launching a duplicate.
- Completion, failure, and cancellation have defined, verifiable user-visible outcomes.
- The chosen turn-completion and restart policies are documented and covered by matching end-to-end scenarios.

## Related work

- #434: original report and evidence; superseded by this feature proposal.
- #439: redirected output buffering. Log buffering is a separate concern; coordinate where progress reporting intersects.
items.title: [Feature] Coordinate long-running offline tasks with Agents across turns

### Background

Follow-up to #96, under the backend migration tracked in #84. This issue carries forward the unfinished scope of #96 for release 0.4.0. Closing #96 is an administrative handover, not a claim that its original acceptance criteria have all passed.

Code review baseline: main at `5a86d0593a887e825d3a3da136f760b62807f797` (2026-10-28). This assessment is based on static inspection, not a fresh full acceptance run.

### Existing behavior to preserve

- Keep the existing Runner and its bwrap / Seatbelt sandbox. Do not switch to jiuwenbox or re-enable JiuwenSwarm host execution/file tools.
- Existing environment, execution and workspace functionality remains available through the legacy API behind the adapter proxy.
- Sandbox network settings already have permission-epoch rotation and persistent-kernel teardown behavior in the legacy API. Preserve and verify it rather than treating it as missing.
- Some L1 contract cases already exist, including sandbox network and package-source settings. The historical claim of 21 uncovered rows must be recalculated against current main.

### Remaining scope

- [ ] Inventory every interface row from #96, including the expanded Runner-specific environment paths. Record its current owner, downstream target, existing coverage and remaining work. Preserve the original interface scope; explicitly justify any row requiring no migration.
- [ ] Complete adapter routing and necessary adaptation for local Runner environments, environment setup/revisions, execution records/status/logs/cancellation, kernel teardown, workspace listing/files/sync/deletion, and local Runner list/detail/connect/probe. Replace reliance on the generic legacy API fallback for this scope with explicit ownership and dispatch; reuse existing implementation where possible instead of rewriting the Runner.
- [ ] Implement the required path rewriting (`/api/environments*` to Runner `/environments*`) and dispatch of `/api/runners/:id/...`, preserving authentication, request/response contracts and errors.
- [ ] Complete `agent-activity` aggregation across Runner executions/transfers, JiuwenSwarm cron/schedules and adapter-owned state, including logs and cancellation. Current main aggregates legacy API stores; that alone does not establish the requested integration.
- [ ] Trace and complete configuration persistence and propagation for sandbox network settings and package-source settings. Verify Runner behavior after saving, permission-epoch rotation and invalidation of previous sandbox authorization where required by #96; preserve existing kernel teardown behavior. Explicitly document the intended epoch behavior for package-source changes and resolve any discrepancy with #91/#96.
- [ ] Evaluate whether the `agent-activity` wrapper can be eliminated; record the conclusion and retain only necessary adaptation.

### Boundaries and dependencies

Local Runner environments, execution and workspace only. Remote-host and NPU implementation remains in #104. Coordinate shared routing/dispatch contracts with that issue without absorbing its scope. Adapter core and settings contracts relate to #87 and #91; downstream consumers include #97 and #102.

The sandbox choice is already settled: retain Runner execution and bwrap / Seatbelt.

items.author: HongyeZhou
items.body:
## Problem

#494 adds `scripts/lib/venv-launchers.mjs` (trampoline replace + runtime DLL copy) with portable unit tests, but:

1. Nothing in-tree calls `replaceVenvTrampolines` / `copyVenvRuntimeDlls` (`assemble-backend.mjs` / bootstrap not present yet).
2. Comments claim a closed loop with `fixVenvHome`, but that helper does not exist — after swapping the launcher, `pyvenv.cfg` `home` can still point at the build machine, so the real `python.exe` still fails off-machine.
3. Tests only compare bytes; they do not spawn `Scripts\python.exe`, so the field failures (entity not found / `0xC0000135`) are not covered.

## Expected

- Call sites in assemble-backend (pack-time) and bootstrap (first-run repair) invoke the module.
- `fixVenvHome` (or equivalent) rewrites `pyvenv.cfg` `home` to the bundled interpreter root.
- A Windows smoke test builds a uv venv, relocates it, spawns `Scripts\python.exe -c "..."`, and asserts exit 0 with `sys.prefix` at the new path.

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — pack-time wiring
- **Preconditions:** Payload contains a uv-created venv whose `Scripts\python.exe` is a trampoline; assemble-backend runs.
- **Steps:** Inspect `Scripts\python.exe` and `pyvenv.cfg` after assemble.
- **Expected / pass:** Launcher is a real CPython stub (no `uv trampoline` marker); `home` points at the bundled python root; runtime DLLs sit beside the launcher.

### Case 2 — first-run bootstrap repair
- **Preconditions:** `dataDir\envs` still has pre-fix trampolines (reinstall with valid unpack stamp).
- **Steps:** Start the shell once on a clean machine without system Python.
- **Expected / pass:** Bootstrap replaces trampolines, copies DLLs, fixes `home`; each venv `python.exe -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"` exits 0.

### Case 3 — Windows spawn smoke (CI or labeled job)
- **Preconditions:** `os:windows` (or equivalent) test runner with a bundled/minimal CPython + uv.
- **Steps:** Create uv venv → move tree → `spawn(Scripts/python.exe, ["-c", "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"])`.
- **Expected / pass:** Exit code 0; printed prefix equals the relocated venv path. Byte-only unit tests alone do not satisfy this case.

## Context

Refs #494, #493. Non-blocking Follow-up from HongyeZhou review of shell.04. #494 should use `Refs #493` until this loop lands (or fold wiring into the same PR).
items.title: [Feature] win-desktop-client: wire venv-launchers + fixVenvHome + Windows spawn smoke

items.author: zhaozhaozz
items.body:
## What happened

`E2E_SWARM_TASK` is a test-only variable. `.ci/run-e2e.sh` exports `E2E_SWARM_TASK=1` whenever the backend is JiuwenSwarm, together with `SCIENCE_AGENT_JIUWENSWARM_SUBAGENTS=task`. Twelve specs then gate on it: `expect(process.env.E2E_SWARM_TASK !== "1", "BLOCKED: …").toBe(false)`. No product code reads it.

The precondition it stands for is real: these journeys exercise sub-agents delegated through the platform `task` tool (sandbox, deliverables, sub-agent cards), and some of them exercise JiuwenSwarm itself. As a switch, though, it does not do that job:

- It is a declaration, not a check. A stack started with `SCIENCE_AGENT_JIUWENSWARM_SUBAGENTS=jiuwenswarm`, the one configuration where the precondition fails, still passes if someone exports `E2E_SWARM_TASK=1`.
- In CI it is always `1` on the default backend, so it never stops anything there.
- It blocks journeys that do not depend on JiuwenSwarm. The built-in (native) loop also delegates through the platform `task` tool, but DRB, TC-E2E-01 and BiomniBench report BLOCKED on it unless the variable is set by hand.
- Anyone running a real journey by hand has to remember it; three benchmark READMEs say so.
- `deepresearchbench-swarm.spec.ts` and `biomnibench-da-swarm.spec.ts` write `backend: "jiuwenswarm"` into their score metrics as a constant, so a native run is labelled as JiuwenSwarm.

## Proposal

- `/health` (and `/api/health`) reports how the stack runs agent turns, from the API's own configuration: `agent: { executor: "jiuwenswarm" | "native", subagents: "task" | "jiuwenswarm" }`. The native loop always delegates through `task`. The API is the component that makes this decision in both modes; the adapter's `/agent/info` does not exist when the stack runs natively.
- One E2E helper reads it. Real research journeys (DRB, TC-E2E-01, BiomniBench) require platform `task` delegation on either executor. Journeys that test JiuwenSwarm's own behaviour (`swarm-*`, `literature-review-*`, `artifact-revision`) also require the `jiuwenswarm` executor. A mismatch is reported as BLOCKED with what the stack actually reported.
- `E2E_SWARM_TASK` is removed from `run-e2e.sh`, the specs and the READMEs.
- Score metrics record the executor the stack reported, not a constant.
- `E2E_SWARM_EXCLUSIVE`, `E2E_SWARM_COMPACTION`, `E2E_LITERATURE_FIXTURE` and `E2E_MCP_FAULT_PROXY` stay. They protect exclusive stacks and fixtures, not the stack's identity.
items.title: [Feature] test(e2e): take the sub-agent precondition from the stack instead of the E2E_SWARM_TASK switch

items.author: hsliuustc0106
items.body:
## Cross-check needed

cc @zhaozhaozz @zy95-12 @HongyeZhou

### Three-layer defaults (important)
These coexist and are easy to conflate:

1. **Schema fallback**: `DEFAULT_SKILL_SELECTION_MODE = "all"` when unset (`packages/schema/src/runtime-settings.ts`).
2. **New Project product default**: `withDefaultProjectSkillSettings` writes `skillSelectionMode: "selected"` + empty `enabledSkillIds` / libraries (Skill Library intent: avoid silently expanding capability).
3. **JiuwenSwarm force-all**: on start, `http/index.ts` calls `store.useEverySkillEverywhere()` so the **effective** mode is `all` while Swarm is the backend (stored `selected` is kept and applies again when switching back to native).

Box smoke on Swarm therefore seeing `all` is **expected**, not accidental.

### Observation (box smoke, 2026-10-24 Asia/Shanghai)
- SHA: `main@9eb45d75`
- Backend: **JiuwenSwarm** (force-all path)
- Model: Zhipu `glm-5.3-flash`
- ~17 shipped skills effective, `thinkingEffort: high`
- Trivial user prompt → **~38k input tokens** (chat/history ≈ **165 bytes**)
- First visible assistant text ≈ **20s** wall

Progressive disclosure is **already implemented** (`docs/en/developer-docs/skill-progressive-disclosure.md`: metadata/path in prompt, body on demand). It does **not** prevent metadata/tool-surface growth when the effective selected set is the whole catalog under `all` / Swarm force-all.

### Questions for maintainers
1. Should end-user UX optimize for **Project `selected`** or accept **Swarm force-all** as the primary path?
2. Is there appetite to change schema DEFAULT, Swarm force-all, or both?
3. Have you seen the same **TTFT / cost** under Swarm vs native?

### Proposed performance watch split (do not mix into one Nightly bucket)
1. **UX / API latency lane** — queue → context → **TTFT** → run wall; short daily probe (`live.mjs ttft` + one real short chat), measure under **both** native and JiuwenSwarm, and under `all` vs `selected`.
2. **Correctness lane (existing L3 ×9)** — tool/files/cancel/etc.; keep **out of** TTFT gates.
3. **Research quality lane (L4 Nightly)** — DRB/Biomni/etc. as quality signal, **not** first-token UX.

### Possible directions (not proposing a fix yet)
- Keep progressive disclosure; also shrink **effective set** under Swarm (or stop force-all)
- Align schema DEFAULT with new-Project `selected`
- Cap / warn when resolved skill metadata size exceeds a threshold
- Surface skill-token cost in Usage / composer

### Non-goals
- Nightly research-bench red streak root-cause (separate)
- Tool-call accuracy eval (separate)

### Test coverage gap
- Unit coverage exists for settings semantics (`store.test.ts`: selected / all / `useEverySkillEverywhere`).
- **No CI gate** on TTFT or skill-token size; `live.mjs ttft()` logs only.
- Progressive disclosure tests do not cap catalog size under `all`.

Cross-check so far: skills-side review agrees the three-layer story; DigitalMate has no parallel issue. Nearby: #508, #93, #141.
items.title: [Bug] Swarm/default skillSelectionMode=all inflates context (~38k tokens) and TTFT (~20s)

items.author: zy95-12
items.body:
## 背景 / 输入

长 EM 任务 `mop_sc`（约 26.5 min）通过重定向写入 `logs/mop_sc.log`。进程全程 ~100% CPU，但日志在 gene select 附近长时间停在很小体积（约 623 B），直到进程退出才刷出大量内容。

## 问题是什么

Python/`print` **块缓冲**（非 TTY）导致：

- 用户与监控误判「卡住」
- Agent 更容易用墙钟定时器提前结束 turn（加剧孤儿作业问题）

## 我们怎么规避的

不以日志增长为唯一心跳；改看 `ps` CPU、RSS、以及最终 `predictions.npy` 是否落盘。事后用 `[TIMED]` 行核对 wall/cpu/RSS。

## 期望应该是什么样

1. 产品拉起的长时间命令默认 `python -u` / `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`，或对重定向日志做行缓冲。
2. Session/job UI 提供进程级心跳（CPU、RSS、最近输出时间），不单靠日志文件 mtime。
3. 文档提示 Agent：长任务应用 unbuffered 或显式 `flush`。
